how: Proposing participation and mapping a plot establish a starter role independently of anyone subsequently joining.
Repeated calls recruit participants to put up their national flag.
The coordinate-bearing call receives the bare affirmative answer Yalla.
Participants choose their national flag as the shared mark.
Participants debate whether the available space makes their flag sufficiently large and visible.
Repeated coordinates and a red-line instruction receive an explicit report of finding the plot and starting.
A later recruitment call publishes coordinates and links a plan described as vertical.
A participant reports finding the plot and starting work.
Participants report the flag nearly done and subsequently claim completion.
Participants weigh a more visible site against the currently available plot without reporting that their current plot was lost.
A reported deletion rejects an alternative site, after which a renewed location request receives coordinates and a specific red-line task.
An enthusiastic participant reports being unable to find the flag while using a mobile device.
The reported device limitation concerns locating this flag and does not demonstrate a general inability to place pixels from a phone.
Published coordinates reach an interested helper only if that helper can locate the work on their device.
The mobile location difficulty does not identify a technical fault, blocked access or a working site fix.
Neither the shared plan nor the mobile difficulty evidences automated placement or spare accounts.
Practical task instructions cannot establish formal command or its absence, and one room cannot test the model's prevalence claim.
A bare correction repairs the shared canvas venue name without an explicit preceding question about what the name means.
The opaque MOI call cannot establish whether someone is identifying a picture, explaining a name or doing something else.

statement: noticing and appreciating another canvas picture
how: A participant appreciates a named game picture without asking or explaining what it means.
A warning that someone is ruining the nearly completed flag shows minimal watchfulness during building.
The warning establishes watchfulness but cannot establish repair, sustained defence or restoration of an earlier known form.
The added claim about keepers undoing planned changes cannot be tested because the warning identifies neither an agreed change nor its repair.
A participant attributes deletion at a proposed location to rainbow people without displaying an investigation.
Attribution names rainbow people at one location but leaves the actor in a later damage warning unidentified.
A visitor requests flag help and later confirms success with thanks after another participant checks the outcome.
The appeal, check and thanks establish requested and acknowledged assistance without proving which helpers placed pixels or caused success.
A participant identifying with another room carries that room's flag-help appeal into the host thread.
The help appeal and thanks show no negotiated border, truce or bargain.
The takeover proposal has no coded response refusing it, restraining attackers or apologising.
Regional thanks do not establish a coalition or mutual defence agreement.
The plot instructions and help appeal do not establish a host granting controlled territory.
The help-request exchange contains no evidenced dispute, disclaimer or stated limit on who may commit the room.
Different coordinates across the threads do not establish a collective move after the room's work was overrun.
A participant explicitly frames the successful outcome and thanks through regional belonging by saying GCC for life.
Regional identification in thanks cannot establish that kinship caused assistance or a continuing alliance.
The takeover proposal does not evidence a quarrel carried from before the canvas.
Saying other flags are too numerous does not establish that a prior rivalry or ideology selected the target.
The flag-building calls provide no evidence of a local April Fools prank framing their reception.
Recruitment calls show no coded regulation of canvas talk in the host room.
A collective claim that we did it celebrates the flag's completion.
An after-close question marks the ending and elicits a report that the neighbouring flag succeeded.
Regional thanks after closure do not propose carrying the joint effort into another project.
The after-close confirmation contests neither an image cleanup nor an account describing the group.
A participant proposes taking over another flag because its kind already has too many instances.
A takeover proposal fits the lower range of an attack call without establishing an enacted attack.
The insult about hearts is one-sided hostile commentary without evidence of a continuing exchange with its named target.
An ensuing reciprocal contest is not evidenced by the hearts complaint and separate takeover proposal.
An objection to visibility does not establish insufficient hands or a canvas judged too full.
Coordinates and a linked image show no chat invitation or reported decision from a chat.
Using shabab and banat in a public coordinate-bearing call does not establish hidden plans, coded strategy or infiltration.
The visitor identifies another room but does not say that seeing the flag brought them to this room.
The completion celebration contains no effort to reach creators, teams, companies or the press.
Appreciating Rocket League and using a playful emoticon in a takeover proposal do not establish a canvas joke taken up by the room.
The flag calls do not evidence founding a new canvas room or faction.
The takeover suggestion contains no coded dispute over offensive words or symbols.
The takeover suggestion and hearts complaint contain no exchange arguing whether covering others is fair.
An unidentified damage warning does not establish a member attacking the flag because they object to canvas posts.
The mobile participant reports difficulty without saying they quit or describing a personal quarrel.
Appreciating another game picture does not establish divided membership in rooms sharing a contested border.
The opening proposal receives explicit agreement and a call to find a spot and start.
A specific red-line instruction receives an answer reporting that the respondent found the plot and started.
The bare affirmative answers a recruitment call without establishing a general preference for acceptance over refusal.
Watchfulness accompanies an almost-complete flag, but the exchange cannot establish that building caused repair or a distinct upkeep stage.
The damage warning does not link watching to a negotiation with neighbours.
The takeover proposal supplies no settled border whose effect on restraint can be tested.
The warning supplies no evidence that defence strain caused automated placement.
Progress and celebration occur in order without a passage establishing the proposed causal connection.
A later report about another flag does not explicitly arise from the earlier celebration.
The outcome confirmation supplies no decision to continue the effort for another purpose.
Location talk does not establish that insufficient hands caused a post-loss relocation.
The linked vertical plan does not show a pixel-level template settling an argued design.
A warning precedes an incoming appeal without showing that local defensive strain caused that appeal.
The help appeal supplies no border bargain that opened a channel for assistance.
The takeover suggestion follows recruitment without saying recruitment caused the proposed attack.
The takeover call has no coded answer refusing it or explaining restraint.
The takeover call has no coded answer invoking a truce or proposing a deal.
The earlier hearts complaint and later flag takeover proposal do not establish one attack producing an ensuing contest with one rival.
The warning and regional thanks do not establish a coalition caused by shared attack.
The calls do not establish a canvas flood causing host-room regulation.
No evidenced agreement, compliance disclaimer or authority dispute in the help exchange permits testing the bounded order claim.
